'''Electrical charge''' is a fundamental property of matter.

== SI Unit ==

The SI unit of electrical charge is '''Coulomb (C)''', named after French physicist [[Person:Charles Augustine de Coulomb|Charles Augustine de Coulomb]].<ref>{{#cite:Q1934}}</ref>

== Charge of subatomic particles ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Particle !! Symbol !! Absolute charge (Coulombs) !! Relative charge (to proton)
|-
| [[proton]] || $p^+$ || $+1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ || +1
|-
| [[neutron]] || $n^0$ || 0 || 0
|-
| [[electron]] || $e^-$ || $-1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ || −1
|}

<ref>{{#cite:Q1791}}</ref><ref>{{#cite:Q1793}}</ref>

== Properties ==

=== Quantisation ===

Any electrical charge is a whole multiple of $e \equiv 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19} C$.<ref>{{#cite:Q1934}}</ref>

i.e.,

$$
\forall Q, Q=ae, a \in Z
$$

=== Restricted type ===

A charge must be either positive or negative.<ref>{{#cite:Q1934}}</ref>

Positive and negative charges can cancel each out, therefore the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of charges of all its elements.<ref>{{#cite:Q1934}}</ref>

i.e.,
$$
Q_{system}=\sum Q_{element}
$$

<blockquote>
'''Warning''': This does not mean the entire system can be always approximated as a point charge of $\sum Q_{elements}$, as the distribution of charges heavily influence the electrostatic behaviour of a system.
</blockquote>

=== Conservation ===

Charge can neither be created or destroyed but only transfered. The amount of charge in any closed system is constant.<ref>{{#cite:Q1934}}</ref>

== Charge density ==

For a thin, long conductor (e.g., electric cable):

$$\text{charge density } \lambda = \frac{dQ}{dL}$$

For a thin surface (e.g., aluminium foil):

$$\text{charge density } \sigma = \frac{dQ}{dA}$$
